st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses legal-malpractice damages arising from discovery and privilege failures, not legal AI’s jagged capabilities, selective deployment, verification requirements, or operating-model redesign. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster proposition.

st.t: Legal malpractice: Error alone cannot establish liability
st.an: Gerber supports the cluster’s core proposition that malpractice requires negligence, causation and substantiated loss rather than error alone. It recognizes corrective fees as a potentially independent injury without requiring a different underlying litigation outcome, while preserving proof of proximate causation, negligence and timeliness. The dissent also supports the cluster’s qualification that this was a contested federal prediction, not a definitive Arkansas Supreme Court holding.
qs: It makes sense that proving a case-within-a-case is not a hard-and-fast requirement because an attorney’s negligence can result in injuries other than a loss in court.

If Gerber can establish on remand that Mitchell Williams was negligent in February 2016 and turning over the last batch of documents proximately caused its injury, then its legal-malpractice claim can move forward.2                                            III.

mo.t: Delegated error: Client relief need not excuse counsel

Lawyer accountability: Discipline and liability remain separate

kp.k: Corrective fees need not depend on litigation outcomes
kp.d: The Eighth Circuit majority predicted that Arkansas law permits recovery of attorney fees incurred attempting to correct prior counsel’s negligence without proving that the underlying litigation would have ended differently. It reversed summary judgment and remanded; it did not award damages or establish that Gerber had proved its claim. The opinion addresses conventional legal malpractice, not AI.
qs: There is no case within a case here because Gerber’s theory has nothing to do with how its state-court lawsuit will turn out.
Instead, it wants to get back the more than $75,000 it spent trying to regain its attorney-client privilege after Mitchell Williams negligently waived it.
We accordingly reverse the judgment of the district court and remand for further proceedings.

kp.k: Privilege-management failures generated attempted remediation costs
kp.d: The majority recounts successive discovery failures: privileged material appeared in an initial 2,700-page production; another 96,000 pages followed without a privilege log; later productions included incomplete or late logs. After privilege was held waived and a protective order denied, Gerber hired replacement counsel whose interlocutory appeal failed. These are the factual circumstances underlying the corrective-fee claim, rather than evidence about technology adoption.
qs: In the initial phases of discovery, Gerber produced 2,700 pages of documents.
After the state trial court granted an unopposed motion to compel, Gerber produced another 96,000 pages of documents. Still no privilege log.

Opposing counsel successfully argued that Gerber had already waived its attorney-client privilege by failing to invoke it in time, producing privileged documents, and creating an incomplete privilege log.

kp.k: Recovery requires a causal link to additional fees
kp.d: The majority retained ordinary negligence causation requirements: Gerber must connect counsel’s negligence to the extra fees through a natural and continuous sequence and show that those fees would not otherwise have been incurred. Allowing a corrective-fee theory therefore does not make every replacement-counsel expense recoverable.
qs: What it requires, in other words, is an unbroken causal chain between an attorney’s negligence and the injury.
If Gerber can also demonstrate that it “would not have incurred the fees in the absence of the [firm’s] negligence,” it will have completed the necessary causal chain.

kp.k: Malpractice injuries extend beyond losing a case
kp.d: The majority distinguished claims seeking compensation for an adverse litigation outcome, where the underlying merits form part of the malpractice proof, from other identifiable monetary injuries. It used the Restatement’s hypothetical negligent disclosure of trade secrets to illustrate business harm that can exist independently of a judgment, and reported that most courts addressing comparable corrective-fee claims supported recovery without an underlying judgment.
qs: It makes sense that proving a case-within-a-case is not a hard-and-fast requirement because an attorney’s negligence can result in injuries other than a loss in court.
Take the Restatement’s example of an attorney’s negligent disclosure of a company’s trade secrets.
Of the few courts that have addressed a situation like this one, most have reached the same conclusion that we do: corrective fees are available, even without an underlying judgment.

kp.k: Limitations run from negligence, not its discovery
kp.d: The court applied Arkansas’s three-year limitations period, making January 15, 2016 the cutoff for this suit. The February 2016 production fell within that period, but Gerber still needed to establish that this production was negligent and proximately caused its injury. Earlier privilege-waiver findings did not determine whether that later production was negligent.
qs: The only acts falling within Arkansas’s three-year statute of limitations were those that occurred on or after January 15, 2016, which was exactly three years before Gerber filed its malpractice suit.
Fortunately for Gerber, one set of documents was turned over in February 2016, just within the three-year period.

If Gerber can establish on remand that Mitchell Williams was negligent in February 2016 and turning over the last batch of documents proximately caused its injury, then its legal-malpractice claim can move forward.

kp.k: Dissent challenges federal prediction of expanded malpractice liability
kp.d: Judge Erickson argued that the novel state-law question should be certified to the Arkansas Supreme Court, even without a party request, or otherwise resolved by deferring to the district judge’s prediction against recovery. He described the claim as exceeding $500,000, whereas the majority described more than $75,000, and stressed the unsuccessful remediation effort and absence of demonstrated harm from disclosure. His concurrence in the majority’s analysis was conditional on Arkansas accepting the expanded recovery theory.
qs: Before I would expose a law firm to this previously uncharted type of malpractice claim with potential damages exceeding $500,000, I would take the rare step of certifying the question to the Arkansas Supreme Court, even though neither party made such a request.

This is particularly so when in this case there has been no showing that the production of a privileged document caused harm to the client and the client chose to pursue what turned out to be a futile, and substantially expensive, endeavor to “claw back” the erroneously produced documents.

If the Arkansas Supreme Court relaxed the case-within-a case requirement for malpractice claims and allowed a client to recover damages outside of a loss in court, such as is set forth in § 53 of the Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers, then I concur in the majority’s analysis.
